                                SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                       PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                                           §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC                                        §
AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                                                §
SERVICES CORPORATION TO                                              §      BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                                          §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                                            §                            OF
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST                                             §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                                        §     ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                                             §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                                             §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                                           §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,                                             §
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN                                            §
SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                                         §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                              §


                INTERVENORS CHARLES E. AND CHERYL L. RAEKE’S
                               REPLY BRIEF

                                           I. INTRODUCTION
       Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief confirms, rather than rebuts, the Raeke Intervenors’
case against Link F41 across Tract 2642. Applicants concede three things that are dispositive. First,
every one of the 122 filed routes—and the alternative routes that avoid Tract 2642—is “viable and
constructible,” and Applicants “will construct the transmission line in accordance with the
Commission’s determination.” Second, Applicants “do not object to the selection of any filed route
or constructible combination of forward-progressing alternative route links.” Third, route selection
is “a balancing of factors” under PURA § 37.056(c) committed to the Commission’s discretion.
Taken together, these concessions mean that selecting an alternative that spares the Raeke
residence imposes no cost, delay, or engineering obstacle on the Project. The only contested
question is which route is best supported by the statutory factors as applied to Tract 2642—and on
that question Applicants’ brief is silent.

       Applicants devote their brief to defending the Project as a whole and to a global comparison
of “routes of interest.” They never engage the tract-specific § 37.056(c) failures the Raekes
documented at hearing: a 765-kV line within 300 feet of an occupied residence, a greenfield
corridor that parallels no existing right-of-way, and a documented, market-tested loss of value to


                         Intervenors Charles E. and Cheryl L. Raeke Reply Brief •   Page 1 of 6


                                                                             Doc ID: d2e1b5e081951937a3bd90a30613629d074cc246
 Tract 2642. Nor do Applicants acknowledge—let alone excuse—their failure to answer the
Raekes’ Requests for Information. The Commission should reject F41 across Tract 2642 and direct
selection of an alternative; in the alternative, it should impose the binding mitigation conditions
set out in the Raekes’ Initial Brief.

II. APPLICANTS’ OWN CONCESSIONS REMOVE ANY OBSTACLE TO AVOIDING
                            TRACT 2642
        Applicants affirmatively represent that they “do not object to the selection of any filed
route or constructible combination of forward-progressing alternative route links,” and that any of
the 122 routes “are viable and constructible.” Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief at 40, 59. That
position is fatal to any argument that F41 must cross Tract 2642. By Applicants’ own admission,
the Commission can select a route that avoids the Raeke residence without sacrificing reliability,
constructability, or the Project schedule, and Applicants will build it.

        Because Applicants are indifferent as among constructible routes, the “best interests of
landowners and the general public” standard of PURA § 37.056(c) is the operative tie-breaker.
Where one alignment places a 765-kV structure within 300 feet of a family home on an intact
agricultural tract and an available alternative does not, the landowner-protective standard resolves
the choice against F41. Applicants offer no reason—cost, reliability, or otherwise—why F41 in
particular must cross Tract 2642, and their concession that all routes are viable forecloses any such
reason now.

     III. APPLICANTS’ “BALANCING, NOT SCORING” ARGUMENT DOES NOT
               ANSWER F41’S FACTOR FAILURES ON TRACT 2642
        Applicants argue at length that route selection is “not a math question” and that the
Commission should reject any “reproducible, weighted scoring methodology.” Applicants’ Initial
Post-Hearing Brief at 41. That argument is directed at a position the Raekes never took. The Raekes
do not ask the Commission to crown a route by arithmetic. Their point is qualitative and is the very
“balancing” Applicants endorse: when the statutory factors are weighed, F41 across Tract 2642
fares worst on the factors that matter most here—proximity to habitable structures, use of existing
rights-of-way, and prudent avoidance.

        Applicants’ own “balancing” framework therefore cuts against them. A reasoned balancing
under § 37.056(c) must confront the record evidence that F41 places a 765-kV line within 300 feet



                          Intervenors Charles E. and Cheryl L. Raeke Reply Brief •   Page 2 of 6


                                                                              Doc ID: d2e1b5e081951937a3bd90a30613629d074cc246
 of the Raeke home and cuts a new greenfield corridor across a contiguous agricultural tract, while
filed alternatives travel along existing utility, roadway, or field-edge corridors. Applicants’ nine-
route comparison table—which reports system-wide totals such as habitable structures within 500
feet and miles of paralleling for entire routes—does not address, and cannot answer, the impact at
the Tract 2642 link level. A balancing that never examines the specific harm to Tract 2642 is not
a balancing at all.

IV. APPLICANTS’ UNEXCUSED FAILURE TO ANSWER THE RAEKES’ RFIs MUST
                    BE CONSTRUED AGAINST THEM
        The Raekes served their First Requests for Information on May 15, 2026. Under SOAH
Order No. 6, responses were due within seven working days. Applicants never served responses.
Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief does not mention this failure, offer any justification for it,
or contend that the requested information was unavailable. The non-response therefore stands
unrebutted.

        The unanswered requests went to the heart of the § 37.056(c) analysis: the routing-factor
scoring and rankings (RFI 1-2); habitable-structure inventories within 300, 500, and 1,000 feet of
each route (RFI 1-3); the route-paralleling tabulation (RFI 1-7); the comparative cost and cost-per-
structure-avoided analysis (RFI 1-12); the environmental and biological analyses (RFI 1-5); the
prudent-avoidance, EMF, and visual-impact analyses (RFI 1-6); and the cumulative-impact studies
(RFI 1-17). Applicants cannot now rely on data tables and exhibits they declined to produce to the
Raekes—such as the combined data tables underlying their route comparison—to carry a burden
that is theirs alone. The burden of proof under § 37.056(c) rests with Applicants, and any gap in
the comparative record created by their discovery default must be construed against them, not
against the landowner.

V. HABITABLE-STRUCTURE PROXIMITY AND PRUDENT AVOIDANCE REMAIN
                         UNANSWERED
        Applicants invoke the Commission’s prudent-avoidance policy in the abstract and assert
generally that all 122 routes comply with it. They offer no evidence specific to the Raeke residence,
which sits within 300 feet of the F41 centerline. The Raekes’ sworn testimony (Ex. 23) that F41
would place permanent 765-kV structures within 300 feet of their home and additional occupied
structures within the 500- and 1,000-foot prudent-avoidance bands is uncontroverted. Because
Applicants withheld their prudent-avoidance, EMF, and visual-impact analyses (RFI 1-6), there is


                         Intervenors Charles E. and Cheryl L. Raeke Reply Brief •   Page 3 of 6


                                                                             Doc ID: d2e1b5e081951937a3bd90a30613629d074cc246
 no record evidence, tested by the Raekes, that F41 satisfies prudent avoidance as applied to Tract
2642. Minimization of impacts on habitable structures is a primary criterion under § 37.056(c) and
16 TAC § 25.101, and on this record F41 fails it more severely on Tract 2642 than any alternative
the Raekes identified.

  VI. DEFERRING ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW TO POST-APPROVAL AGENCY
         CONSULTATION DOES NOT CURE THE ROUTING RECORD
       Applicants respond to environmental concerns by pointing to standard ordering paragraphs
and to consultations—with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under the Endangered Species Act,
and with the Texas Historical Commission—that, by Applicants’ own account, will occur only
“following the Commission’s approval” of the Project. Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief at
55–57. Post-approval consultation cannot substitute for considering environmental constraints at
the routing stage, which is when § 37.056(c) requires the effect on the environment to be weighed.
The Raekes’ unrebutted testimony documents Texas Horned Lizard habitat and drainage features
along the F41 corridor on Tract 2642, and Applicants withheld their environmental-constraints and
biological analyses (RFI 1-5). Choosing a route first and studying its environmental effects later
inverts the statutory sequence.

      VII. THE REQUESTED MITIGATION CONDITIONS ARE MODEST AND
               CONSISTENT WITH APPLICANTS’ OWN POSITION
       Applicants state that they “do not object” to the Commission’s standard ordering
paragraphs governing environmental compliance and agency coordination. The binding conditions
the Raekes request, should F41 be approved over their tract, are of the same modest character and
should be imposed: minimum tower setbacks from the residence and occupied outbuildings to the
extent engineering permits; pre-construction survey and post-construction monitoring of the Tract
2642 water well at Applicants’ expense, with a duty to restore or replace it; a pre-construction
Texas Horned Lizard and harvester-ant survey with appropriate avoidance measures; access-road
placement that minimizes disruption to the goat operation; restoration of disturbed agricultural
land at Applicants’ expense; and written notice to the Raekes’ counsel at least 30 days before
construction. Applicants identify no burden these conditions would impose, and none is apparent.




                         Intervenors Charles E. and Cheryl L. Raeke Reply Brief •   Page 4 of 6


                                                                             Doc ID: d2e1b5e081951937a3bd90a30613629d074cc246
                VIII. THE DAMAGES RECORD STANDS UNCONTESTED
       Applicants do not contest the Raekes’ record on harm to Tract 2642. The documented May
22, 2026 termination of the Raekes’ pending sale—after the buyer received Oncor’s utility-
disclosure packet identifying the F41 corridor—together with the relisting without interest and
realtor Wade Gordy’s testimony on marketability, remains unrebutted. As explained in the Raekes’
Initial Brief, this evidence is preserved for any subsequent condemnation proceeding under
Chapter 21 of the Texas Property Code and is not waived by its inclusion here.

                                IX. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
       Applicants’ brief shows that an alternative to F41 across Tract 2642 is available,
constructible, and unopposed by Applicants. The Raeke Intervenors respectfully request that the
Commission: (1) decline to approve Link F41 as it crosses Tract 2642 and require selection of an
alternative route that avoids the tract or materially reduces impacts on habitable structures,
agricultural use, and the Raekes’ water supply; (2) in the alternative, impose the binding mitigation
conditions set forth in the Raekes’ Initial Brief as a condition of any order approving F41; (3)
preserve for the administrative record all testimony and exhibits concerning damages to Tract
2642; and (4) grant such other and further relief to which the Raekes are justly entitled.

                                                           Respectfully submitted,

                                                           The Law Office of M. Bryon Barnhill, PLLC
